 1                           I. STAFF INTRODUCTION

 2   Q.   Please state your name and business address.

 3   A.   My name is Ed Rilkoff. My business address is the New Mexico Public Regulation

 4        Commission (“Commission”, “NMPRC”, or “PRC”), 1596 Pacheco Street, Santa

 5        Fe, NM 87505.

 6

 7   Q.   What is your position with the Commission?

 8   A.   I am Senior Policy Advisor in the Office of the Chief of Staff at the NMPRC.

 9

10   Q.   Please briefly summarize your education and experience.

11   A.   I have more than 25 years of experience in the energy industry, including utility

12        regulation, energy policy, natural gas and electric markets, commercial

13        transactions, and power project development. I currently serve as Senior Policy

14        Advisor at the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission and previously served

15        as Director of Utilities. Before joining the Commission, I worked for an

16        independent power producer, a major New England electric utility, and the Alberta

17        Department of Energy, with responsibilities involving power marketing, fuel

18        supply strategy, and economic analysis. I hold an MBA from Northeastern

19        University, an M.A. in Economics from the University of Alberta, and a B.Sc. in

20        Mathematics from the University of Alberta.

                                                    ED RILKOFF
                                          NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00079-UT


 1   Q.       Have you previously testified before this Commission?

 2   A.       Yes, I previously testified before this Commission in Case No. 22-00309-UT.

 3

 4   Q.       What is the purpose of your direct testimony in this case?

 5   A.       The purpose of my testimony is to address the affordability implications of SPS's

 6            requested rate increase. My testimony focuses on the relationship between

 7            affordability, projected load growth, rate class cost responsibility, and bill impacts.

 8            It also addresses whether, from an affordability perspective, SPS's proposed class

 9            revenue allocation and rate design should be approved as filed in accordance with

10            the Commission’s statutory requirement to ensure fair, just and reasonable rates

11            and safe, reliable electric service1. Staff witness Larry Blank sponsors the detailed

12            jurisdictional allocation, class revenue allocation, banding, and rate-design

13            recommendations, including his review of SPS’s class cost-of-service study. Other

14            Staff witnesses sponsor additional revenue requirement and cost recovery

15            recommendations. My testimony supports those recommendations from an

16            affordability and customer impact perspective.

17

18   Q.       Has Staff included any exhibits in their testimony?

 5        II. SUMMARY OF TESTIMONY AND RECOMMENDATIONS

 6

 7   Q.    Please summarize your testimony and recommendations.

 8   A.    SPS’s own testimony shows that projected sales growth is concentrated in

 9         Commercial and Industrial load, driven substantially by oil and gas related growth

10         and electrification in southeast New Mexico. At the same time, SPS proposes

11         average bill increases of approximately 23.5% for Residential customers, 22.2%

12         for Residential Heating customers, 23.0% for Small General customers, and 23.9%

13         for Secondary General customers.

14         In Staff’s view, those bill impacts raise significant affordability concerns.

15         Residential and smaller non-residential customers should not bear unreasonable

16         increases where the record shows that much of the projected growth pressure is

17         concentrated in larger Commercial and Industrial load.

18         From an affordability perspective, I support Staff witness Larry Blank’s

19         recommendations regarding jurisdictional allocation, class revenue allocation,


                                               5
                                               DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                                     ED RILKOFF
                                           NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00079-UT


 1              banding, rate design, and SPS’s proposed Electric Affordability Program.2 I also

 2              support the revenue requirement and cost-recovery recommendations sponsored by

 3              other Staff witnesses to the extent those recommendations reduce the amount that

 4              must be recovered from customers or avoid shifting additional costs to customers.

 5              My testimony does not sponsor the technical class cost-of-service, banding, or rate-

 6              design calculations. Rather, my testimony explains why Staff’s recommendations

 7              are important from an affordability and customer-impact perspective.

 8              Figure 1 below compares SPS’s projected sales growth by customer group with the

 9              proposed bill increases for the related rate classes. The graph shows that Residential

10              and Small C&I customers have relatively low projected growth, at 0.5 percent and

11              2.5 percent, but face bill increases of roughly 22 percent to 24 percent. By contrast,

12              Large C&I shows higher projected growth, at 14.0 percent, while the proposed

13              increases for those classes vary widely. Overall, the graph highlights that the

4   In Staff’s view, affordability in this case should be addressed through class

5   allocation and rate design, not only through a targeted low-income assistance

6   mechanism. SPS’s proposed Electric Affordability Program may provide

7   supplemental relief to certain low-income customers, but it does not replace the

8   need to set fair class allocations and reasonable rates.

 1   Q.   Does the Governor’s Executive Order on energy affordability and grid

 2        modernization provide relevant context for your testimony?

 3   A.   Yes. Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham’s Executive Order 2026-023 highlights

 4        statewide concern about rising energy costs and the need to protect ratepayers while

 5        maintaining reliable electric service. I reference the Executive Order as policy

 6        context. Consistent with that context, my recommendations are based on the record

 7        evidence, including SPS’s projected load growth, the proposed bill impacts by

 8        customer class, the ratemaking and other recommendations of Staff witness Larry

 9        Blank and other Staff witnesses, and the Commission’s obligation to ensure fair,

10        just, and reasonable rates and safe, reliable electric service.

11

12   Q.   Are there other ways to mitigate bill impacts to residential ratepayers besides

13        rate allocation?

14   A.   Yes. Customer bill impacts can also be mitigated through Staff recommendations

15        that reduce the overall revenue requirement or avoid shifting additional cost risk to

16        customers. Other Staff witnesses sponsor recommendations regarding revenue

17        requirement, cost recovery, Long Term Power Purchase Agreement (LTPPA)

18        related costs, off-system sales margins, proposed trackers, return on equity, capital

19        structure, and other issues. I rely on those witnesses for the specific technical

20        recommendations. From an affordability perspective, recommendations that reduce

 1           the approved revenue requirement or avoid unnecessary cost shifting to customers

 2           are important because they reduce the pressure on customer bills.

 3

 4   Q.       How do Staff witness Blank’s recommendations address the affordability

 5           concerns discussed in your testimony?

 6   A.       Staff witness Blank’s recommendations address affordability in several ways.

 7           First, his jurisdictional allocation recommendation addresses whether New Mexico

 8           retail customers are being assigned an appropriate share of SPS’s system costs.

 9           Staff witness Blank estimates that his recommendation would reduce SPS’s New

10           Mexico revenue deficiency by approximately $56.7 million, and his testimony

11           provides the calculation and technical support for that estimate.3 Second, his class

12           revenue allocation and banding recommendations provide a technical ratemaking

13           approach for producing a more balanced distribution of the approved revenue

14           increase than SPS’s as-filed proposal.4 Third, his recommendation to limit the

15           Residential Service Availability Charge to $15.00 moderates the fixed monthly

16           charge paid by residential customers. Fourth, his recommendation regarding SPS’s

17           proposed Electric Affordability Program allows targeted assistance to begin while

18           limiting uncertainty about the cost shifted to other customers.5

 1   Q.   What Staff recommendations do you support from an affordability

 2        perspective?

 3   A.   From an affordability perspective, Staff does not support SPS’s proposed class

 4        revenue allocation and rate design as-filed and recommends that the Commission

 5        adopt the class allocation, banding, and specific rate-design recommendations

 6        sponsored by Staff witness Larry Blank. Staff also recommends that the

 7        Commission consider the revenue requirement and cost-recovery recommendations

 8        sponsored by other Staff witnesses because those recommendations may reduce

 9        customer bill impacts. Any approved Electric Affordability Program should be

10        treated as supplemental relief, not as a substitute for fair class allocation and

11        reasonable rate design.

12


13                    III. AFFORDABILITY FRAMEWORK

14

15   Q.   What do you mean by affordability in this case?

16   A.   Affordability in this case is broader than low-income assistance. It includes whether

17        proposed bill impacts are reasonably absorbable for households and businesses and

18        whether the costs driving those increases are fairly assigned among customer

19        classes.


                                                10
                                     DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                          ED RILKOFF
                                 NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00079-UT


 1        Affordability and cost causation should be considered together. Where major

 2        system investment is being driven by concentrated growth in larger customer

 3        classes, the Commission should carefully examine whether the resulting revenue

 4        allocation places too much burden on customers who are not the primary drivers of

 5        that growth.

 6        Smaller customers warrant special attention. Residential, Residential Heating,

 7        Small General, and Secondary General customers generally have less flexibility to

 8        absorb large increases than large commercial and industrial customers.

 9

10   Q.   Is affordability only a residential issue?

11   A.   No. Residential affordability is important, but it is not the only affordability issue

12        in this case. Small commercial and smaller non-residential customers may also have

13        limited ability to absorb large increases. Many small businesses are employers and

14        may have less ability than larger customers to absorb higher electric costs or pass

15        those costs through to customers. As a result, large rate increases can place pressure

16        on small business margins and operations. Larger customers raise different

17        affordability issues involving competitiveness, fuel substitution, and the

18        appropriate assignment of growth-related costs.

19



                                               11
                                     DIRECT TESTIMONY OF
                                          ED RILKOFF
                                 NMPRC CASE NO. 25-00079-UT


 1   Q.   Why do affordability and cost causation need to be considered together?

 2   A.   Because the central question in this case is not simply whether SPS needs additional

 3        investment, but also who should pay for it and who caused the increased costs to

 4        the system. If the major system pressures are being driven by concentrated large-

 5        load growth, then customers who are not primarily responsible for that growth

 6        should not be required to carry an unreasonable share of the resulting rate increase.

 7


 8        IV. GROWTH, COST CAUSATION, AND CLASS IMPACTS

 9

10   Q.   What does the record show about projected load growth?

11   A.    The record shows that projected growth is concentrated in Commercial and

12        Industrial load. Zoë Lees states that retail sales growth is driven mainly by

13        expanding Commercial and Industrial loads, particularly continued oil and gas

14        growth and electrification in southeast New Mexico. John Goodenough likewise

15        states that expected sales growth is largely driven by growth in the Commercial and

16        Industrial classes due to expansion of the oil and gas industry in southeast New

17        Mexico. Casey Meeks also states that the largest factor contributing to distribution

 1              growth in New Mexico is oil-and-gas-related growth, including electrification of

 2              oil and gas production processes.6

 3

 4   Q.         Does the record quantify the class growth pattern?

 5   A.         Yes. Goodenough's class growth summary shows Future Test Year sales growth

 6              of approximately 0.5% for Residential, 2.5% for Small C&I, and 14.0% for Large

 7              C&I. Those figures show that the major growth pressures in this case are not spread

 8              evenly across all classes.7

 9              Projected growth is not the only basis for class revenue allocation. Class cost-of-

10              service results, banding, rate design principles, and judgment also matter. Staff

11              witness Blank sponsors the specific class revenue allocation and banding

12              recommendations. My testimony addresses the affordability implications of SPS’s

13              proposed bill impacts.

14

 7       V. WHY SPS’S AS-FILED ALLOCATION SHOULD BE MODIFIED

 8

 9              For purposes of my testimony, the customer classes at issue generally fall into two

10              broad groups. Residential and Residential Heating customers are household

11              customers. Small General and Secondary General are smaller non-residential

12              classes, including smaller business customers and other customers served at lower

13              distribution voltage levels. Primary General and the LGS-T classes are larger non-

14              residential classes served at higher voltage levels, with the LGS-T classes

15              representing the largest transmission-level retail customers such as a large oil and

16              gas or industrial customer taking service at transmission voltage. In general, as

17              service moves from Secondary General to Primary General to LGS-T, the

 6   Q.    What is your overall view of those bill impacts?

 7   A.    Staff does not support them as filed. The proposed increases for residential and

 8         smaller customer classes raise affordability concerns because the record shows that

13        VI. STAFF RECOMMENDATIONS ON RATE DESIGN AND

14                                   RECOVERY ISSUES

17         and rate design?

 1                 VII. OTHER RATE DESIGN AND COST RECOVERY

 4   Q.         Do Staff witness Christopher E. Dunn’s recommendations also address

 5              affordability?

 6   A.          Yes. Staff witness Christopher E. Dunn recommends a ROE of 9.75%, a capital

 7              structure of 54.76% equity and 45.24% long-term debt, and an overall rate of return

 8              of 7.7323%, compared with SPS’s requested ROE of 10.50%, proposed equity ratio

 9              of 56.00%, and proposed overall rate of return of 8.21%.17 I rely on Staff witness

10              Dunn for the technical support for those recommendations. From an affordability

11              perspective, I support those recommendations because they reasonably balance

12              SPS’s opportunity to earn a fair return with the need to protect customers from

13              unnecessary rate increases.

14   Q.         Do Staff witness Peterson Brossy’s recommendations also address

15              affordability?

16   A.         Yes. Staff witness Peterson Brossy presents Staff’s adjusted revenue requirement,

17              which reduces SPS’s original requested revenue deficiency from approximately

18              $175.4 million, or 24.45%, to approximately $47.7 million, or 6.65%.18 Staff

 2   Q.        Does Staff have a recommendation regarding SPS’s recovery of SPP deficiency

 3             payments?

 4   A.        Yes. Staff witness Jonah Mauldin recommends that the Commission deny SPS’s

 5             request to recover projected SPP deficiency payments through the Fuel and

 6             Purchased Power Cost Adjustment Clause, or FPPCAC, and does not support

 7             recovery of those costs from customers through a tracker or alternative mechanism

 8             in this proceeding.21

 9

10   Q.        Why do you support that recommendation from an affordability perspective?

11   A.        Projected deficiency payments should not be shifted to customers without adequate

12             review. From an affordability perspective, customers should not bear costs that may

13             be related to planning or compliance shortfalls, particularly where the costs have

14             not yet been incurred and the issue is therefore not ripe for Commission

15             consideration at this time.
